claims.claim: Microsoft Learn labels DirectShow a legacy feature that Media Foundation capture has superseded. It strongly recommends that new code use MF capture and that existing DirectShow code be rewritten. The same banner appears on the capture-relevant DirectShow pages: Smart Tee, Time Stamps and MJPEG Decompressor.
claims.evidence: "DirectShow, is a legacy feature. It has been superseded by MediaPlayer, IMFMediaEngine, and Audio/Video Capture in Media Foundation. Those features have been optimized for Windows 10 and Windows 11. Microsoft strongly recommends that new code use ... Audio/Video Capture in Media Foundation instead of DirectShow, when possible. Microsoft suggests that existing code that uses the legacy APIs be rewritten to use the new APIs if possible."

claims.claim: Microsoft's own driver documentation calls the DirectShow capture pipeline 'in maintenance mode'. It says the DirectShow pipeline lags behind the MF pipeline, which gets the new OS features.
claims.evidence: "The modern pipeline is more thoroughly documented and utilizes the features added to the OS over the multiple releases. The legacy pipeline, being in maintenance mode, lags behind."

claims.claim: A 'DShow Bridge' routes DirectShow capture through the MF pipeline and Frame Server, but each UVC device must opt in with the EnableDshowRedirection value (bit 0x1). Only with that opt-in can a DirectShow app share the camera with other apps.
claims.evidence: "DShow Bridge was written with the intent of bridging the DShow pipeline with Media Foundation platform ... on Windows version 1607 and later. With DShow Bridge opt-in enabled, a DShow application and sharing applications can share the same camera hardware concurrently." The registry value is DWORD EnableDshowRedirection under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB\<VID&PID>\<Instance>\Device Parameters, where 0x00000001 means "Opt into DShow Bridge".

claims.claim: Bit 0x2 of the same opt-in tells Frame Server to decode MJPEG once and offer YUY2 instead. For a camera opted in this way, bridged DirectShow apps would see no MJPEG media type.
claims.evidence: "0x00000002 | Enable MJPEG decoding once in FrameServer ... 1 – Expose the translated uncompressed media types from MJPEG (YUY2)"

claims.claim: Chromium's DirectShow path has a weaker timestamp source than its MF path. DirectShow uses only IMediaSample start time, relative to stream time, and falls back to wall clock when it is missing. The MF path reads the device's capture QPC time (MFSampleExtension_DeviceReferenceSystemTime).
claims.evidence: sink_input_pin_win.cc: "if (SUCCEEDED(sample->GetTime(&start_time, &end_time))) { timestamp = base::Microseconds(start_time / 10); }". video_capture_device_win.cc: "There is a chance that the platform does not provide us with the timestamp, in which case, we use reference time ... timestamp = base::TimeTicks::Now() - first_ref_time_;". video_capture_device_mf_win.cc: "sample->GetUINT64(MFSampleExtension_DeviceReferenceSystemTime, &raw_capture_begin_time)".

claims.claim: Microsoft documents that DirectShow preview-pin frames carry no timestamps. For single-pin cameras such as UVC webcams, the Smart Tee that splits capture and preview strips timestamps from the preview stream and delivers preview frames only when that does not hurt capture.
claims.evidence: Time Stamps: "Video frames from a preview pin (as opposed to a capture pin) are not time stamped." Smart Tee: "The Smart Tee filter delivers preview data only if doing so does not hurt capture performance. It also removes the time stamps from the preview stream. The capture graph builder automatically inserts the Smart Tee filter when needed."

claims.claim: OpenCV's CAP_DSHOW backend, skellycam's current path, structurally throws away DirectShow timestamps. It builds a PREVIEW-pin graph, sets the graph clock to NULL, ignores the SampleTime argument in SampleCB, and requests RGB24 from the Sample Grabber, which forces a decoder such as the MJPEG Decompressor into the graph. So CAP_DSHOW timing problems belong to OpenCV's graph design, not necessarily to DirectShow itself.
claims.evidence: cap_dshow.cpp (4.x): "hr = VD->pCaptureGraph->RenderStream(&PIN_CATEGORY_PREVIEW, &MEDIATYPE_Video, VD->pVideoInputFilter, VD->pGrabberF, VD->pDestFilter);"; "//EXP - lets try setting the sync source to null - and make it run as fast as possible ... pMediaFilter->SetSyncSource(NULL);"; "STDMETHODIMP SampleCB(double , IMediaSample *pSample)" (time unused); "mt.subtype = MEDIASUBTYPE_RGB24; //Making it RGB24, does conversion from YUV to RGB".

claims.claim: FFmpeg's dshow input historically ignored DirectShow device video timestamps because they were considered unreliable. Since 2021-12-24 (FFmpeg 5.0+) it uses device timestamps by default and keeps workarounds for missing or garbage sample times.
claims.evidence: Commit 7dc33aad, 2021-12-24: "The dshow avdevice ignores timestamps for video frames provided by the DirectShow device, instead using wallclock time, apparently because the implementer of this code had a device that provided unreliable timestamps ... this patch sets the default to using the device timestamps". dshow_pin.c: "/* PTS from video devices is unreliable. */"; "frame with missing sample timestamp encountered, falling back to graph timestamp"; "initial frames sometimes start < 0 ... For now just drop them." Docs: "This allows working around devices that provide unreliable timestamps."

claims.claim: In this repo's own Windows tests, PyAV/FFmpeg dshow pts were nominal 33.333 ms steps that drifted 1.42 s from arrival in 10 s on the generic camera. MF llTimestamp matched the device timestamp on 100% of frames and carried the UVC payload header on the C922 and C930e.
claims.evidence: "MF is preferred over PyAV dshow because it also carries usable timestamps: llTimestamp equals the device timestamp on 100% of frames, and the 32-byte UVC payload header arrives on the C922 and C930e. PyAV's pts are nominal 33.333 ms steps, so on the generic camera they drift 1.42 s from arrival in 10 s. PyAV remains a working fallback with byte-identical output."

claims.claim: PyAV/FFmpeg dshow with vcodec=mjpeg is a working native-JPEG path. Its JPEG headers are byte-identical to MF's, it delivers full frame rate, and it costs about 1-2% of one CPU core. On byte delivery alone, DirectShow is not worse than MF.
claims.evidence: "PyAV / FFmpeg dshow with `vcodec=mjpeg` (demux only) is a second native path. Its JPEG headers are byte-identical to MF's for every camera and mode." Table: PyAV dshow 720p30: 30.04 / 30.04 / 25.74 fps, 100% valid, 0.9 / 1.3 / 1.3% CPU.

claims.claim: FFmpeg, and therefore PyAV, has no Media Foundation camera input. dshow is its only modern Windows camera demuxer, so a pure-Python, no-compile route to native JPEG bytes on Windows is DirectShow.
claims.evidence: ffmpeg-devices documentation lists dshow, vfwcap and gdigrab as the Windows inputs. Fetched page summary: "The document does not mention a Media Foundation camera input."

claims.claim: FFmpeg dshow drops frames itself when its real-time buffer (rtbufsize) fills, using a probabilistic drop score. A slow consumer silently loses frames, which are logged only as errors.
claims.evidence: dshow.c shall_we_drop(): "real-time buffer [%s] [%s input] too full or near too full (%d%% of size: %d [rtbufsize parameter])! frame dropped!" with dropscore[] = {62, 75, 87, 100}.

claims.claim: Multi-camera USB bandwidth failures look the same on DirectShow and MF. In local tests, a second MJPEG camera on a shared USB 2.0 hub failed on both stacks, so DirectShow gives no bandwidth advantage. Public DirectShow reports show the same class of error.
claims.evidence: Local: "One MJPEG camera per shared USB 2.0 hub at 720p or 1080p. The second camera fails (MF 0x800718CF, DirectShow OSError 5); with a 2.5 s stagger the second always loses." OBS forum, 2020-06-14: "DShow: Run failed (0x800705AA): Insufficient system resources exist to complete the requested service." Fixed by "not connecting via hub".

claims.claim: DirectShow format negotiation through OpenCV is order-fragile. Setting FOURCC before size gave YUY2 at about 10 fps, while setting size first gave MJPG at 30 fps, and neither ordering returned JPEG bytes.
claims.evidence: "OpenCV DSHOW CONVERT_RGB=0 gives YUY2 at 10 fps | ... size-first order gives MJPG at 30 fps, still BGR | Weakened: fourcc-first reproduces YUY2 at 9.99 fps | Depends on property order; neither returns JPEG"

claims.claim: DirectShow apps were not insulated from Frame Server in Windows 10 1607. The Anniversary Update change that removed MJPEG and H.264 broke DirectShow-based apps such as Skype and Kinovea, so 'DS is more reliable than MF' did not hold during that incident.
claims.evidence: Kinovea admin, 2016-08-23: "a recent auto-update of Windows 10 is breaking MJPEG streams for applications based on DirectShow"; "they moved the decoding stage upstream in the pipeline and removed access to the compressed stream"; "breaking many high profile applications like Skype". Thurrott, 2016-08-19: "Windows no longer allows USB webcams to use MJPEG or H264 encoded streams and is only allowing YUY2 encoding"; the workaround was EnableFrameServerMode=0.

claims.claim: The Windows 11 Settings 'Video rotation' option strips MJPEG and H.264 from a camera. Microsoft warns that legacy apps that depend on compressed types may break, and the setting is a user-side risk for any MJPEG-dependent capture path. Settings default image values are applied whenever an app starts the camera.
claims.evidence: "When Video rotation is set to any value other than No rotation, Windows removes all compressed data types, for example, MJPEG, and H.264, from the camera and strictly outputs uncompressed data types. Legacy applications and cameras that depend on compressed data types being available might not function correctly". Also: "When an application opens and starts the camera, Windows starts the camera and then applies any default values to the camera."

claims.claim: Windows Studio Effects only applies to NPU-equipped devices and the integrated front-facing camera. It is irrelevant to external USB mocap webcams whichever API is used.
claims.evidence: "Windows Studio Effects utilizes AI on select Windows devices with compatible Neural Processing Units (NPUs) to apply special effects to the device camera (currently supports front-facing camera)". Prerequisite: Windows 11 22H2 (Build 22623.885+). "Effects are applied at the hardware level ... it is on by default for any app using the camera".

claims.claim: New Windows camera AI features reach OBS only through an MF capture source, because OBS's existing Video Capture Device is DirectShow-based. Intel had to write a separate MF-based source, and that PR is still open. A 2025 community PR also cited cameras that DirectShow cannot open.
claims.evidence: PR #10471 (Intel, 2024-04-02): "Because this capture device is based on Media Foundation, we created separate 'Video Capture Device 2'. We are thinking that it's better to integrate it into the existing DShow based Video Capture Device". PR #12816 (2025-11-13, closed as a duplicate): "Some cameras do not open by dshow."

claims.claim: On Windows on ARM, DirectShow filters are per-architecture COM registrations. OBS's DirectShow virtual camera stayed invisible to native ARM64 apps until users manually registered the ARM64 DLL. A DirectShow-based capture or extension stack needs separate x64 and ARM64 builds and registrations, while MF/Frame Server sources are brokered by the OS.
claims.evidence: OBS forum thread, Jan 2025 to Jan 2026, Snapdragon/ARM64 users: workaround "regsvr32.exe /i /s obs-virtualcam-module-arm64.dll", after which it "worked for Zoom's ARM version" while "MS Teams worked under x64 emulation".

claims.claim: An old OpenCV bug reports image artifacts when MJPG was decoded through CAP_DSHOW on Logitech C920 and ELP cameras at non-default resolutions.
claims.evidence: Issue #11324 (2018-04-16, OpenCV 3.2.0, Win10 64-bit): "Accessing my (physical) webcam compressed by setting the FOURCC to MJPG works ... but adds artifacts to the image on all tested devices ... the last row is completely black". CV_DSHOW was "the only interface I could successfully set MJPG for".

claims.claim: The Microsoft MJPEG Decompressor that DirectShow inserts automatically handles only the 'MJPG' FOURCC and has no documented threading or performance characteristics.
claims.evidence: "This filter is compatible with motion JPEG video that uses the FOURCC code 'MJPG'. It cannot decode other varieties of motion JPEG." Executable quartz.dll, merit MERIT_NORMAL.

claims.claim: DirectShow still ships and is still serviced in current Windows 11 builds. The local qcap.dll carries a recent servicing build number, so there is no sign of removal despite the legacy label.

claims.claim: Device MFT (DMFT) driver extensions are MF components that the device-source pipeline loads. Microsoft recommends that DMFT outputs be NV12 or YUY2 rather than MJPEG. Cameras that ship a vendor DMFT may therefore expose no MJPEG to MF apps, which is a possible MF-side caveat; none of the skellycam cameras registers a CameraDeviceMftClsid.
claims.evidence: "We recommended that the Device MFT produce output media types using NV12 format. YUY2 is the next best alternative. MJPEG and RGB media types aren't recommended." "On 64-bit systems that don't make use of Frame Server, both 32-bit and 64-bit DMFTs must be registered." Local interface registry for the C922, C930e and 4C4A:4A55 lists CLSID, FriendlyName, ExtensionDLL, RTCFlags, FilterData, MSCameraFlags and MetadataBufferSizeInKB0, with no CameraDeviceMftClsid.

gaps: I found no Microsoft document that says whether non-bridged DirectShow apps receive Windows 11 features: Settings > Camera default values, Studio Effects, multi-app camera sharing, or Video rotation. The registry evidence (no EnableDshowRedirection, classic ksproxy filter) suggests DirectShow opens these USB cameras directly and bypasses Frame Server, but that is inferred, not documented.

It is unknown whether the Windows 11 'Allow multiple apps' toggle affects or blocks non-bridged DirectShow apps, and whether its 'single MediaType' would be uncompressed, which would remove MJPEG for MF apps too.

I could not read Microsoft's original 2016 forum explanation (Mike M) of the 1607 Frame Server MJPEG change, so it is cited only through press and the Kinovea admin. FFmpeg trac ticket #8620 and the ffmpeg-devel list archive were blocked by Anubis bot protection; I used the GitHub commit message instead.
I found no authoritative statement of DirectShow capture support or limits on ARM64. The only evidence is OBS anecdotes about per-architecture filter registration.
The network/ONVIF camera doc says 'any camera application may stream from them' but does not say whether DirectShow apps can see them.

I found no primary source showing that DirectShow handles multi-camera USB bandwidth differently from MF. Both sit on usbvideo.sys, and local tests show symmetric failures (MF 0x800718CF vs DirectShow OSError 5).
I found no documented performance or threading data for the inbox DirectShow MJPEG Decompressor.
I found no published Microsoft timeline for removing DirectShow. It is labelled legacy and 'maintenance mode', yet still serviced in build 26100.

I did not measure DirectShow device timestamps directly, that is, IMediaSample::GetTime on a capture pin with a running graph clock. Local evidence covers only the PyAV dshow pts drift, so whether a custom DirectShow capture-pin graph gives timestamps as good as MF llTimestamp is still open.
Chromium's MF blocklist names specific devices (LifeCam Studio, HP HD Camera, and others) but I did not open the linked crbug entries to read the failure modes or the Windows versions involved.

verified.claim: Raw MF IMFSourceReader (native MJPG, converters disabled) delivered the camera's own JPEG at full rate, 100% valid, 0 gaps, on all three cameras, single and multi-camera, at 0.7-2.2% of one core.

It delivered C922 30.00, C930e 30.05 and generic 25.76-25.78 fps (300/301/257-258 frames per 10 s, 0 gaps over 1.5 periods), 100% valid under the lenient decode, at 0.7-2.1% of one core for the capture process (Frame Server excluded). Every streaming test window was 10 s. The generic camera's 1080p frames fail strict libjpeg-turbo decoding on every frame, on MF and PyAV alike. In the 3-camera cells one shared-hub camera was refused bandwidth.

That is the camera's own encoder output, not a re-encode. Rates match MF: C922 30.0, C930e 30.04-30.05, generic 25.74. verified.claim: After vetoed pnputil restarts left DN_NEED_RESTART on camera interface devnodes, every MF open failed with MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED while PyAV DirectShow still captured 192 MJPEG frames from the C922.
verified.corrected_claim: On 2026-10-25, MetadataBufferSizeInKB0=5 was written at 14:09:33 local to enable MF's UVC metadata. The follow-up pnputil /restart-device then returned 3010 ('System reboot is needed'), with LogiTuneAgent vetoing removal (Kernel-PnP 225). That left DN_NEED_RESTART (0x0180610A) on the camera MI_00 devnodes. PyAV DirectShow still captured 192 valid MJPEG frames from the C922 at 14:11:50 local. A replug cleared it.

It is self-inflicted setup, not spontaneous MF flakiness, and it would recur when that metadata registry value is enabled on a user machine running LogiTune. Only one DirectShow cell (C922) ran in the window.

That one observation suggests only the interface flag blocks MF.

verified.claim: The Kiyo Pro EP0 firmware fault breaks every API equally; when healthy, MF and PyAV DirectShow both streamed it.

DirectShow paths failed at open or graph build (PyAV OSError 5 or RenderStream; OpenCV DSHOW 'open failed'). OpenCV MSMF opened and then failed at grab. A health check on MF therefore has to read at least one sample.

verified.claim: MF's bandwidth refusal is specific (0x800718CF, Win32 6351) while FFmpeg DirectShow gives only OSError(5) and OpenCV DSHOW only 'open failed'.

So the generic text partly reflects how the harness captured logs, and a custom DirectShow graph would see the RenderStream HRESULT.

claims.claim: The 'system clock only updates every ~15.6 ms unless you run a program (often a small C# tool) that raises the timer resolution' story is real, but it is designed behavior, not a bug. DateTime.UtcNow, which wraps GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, only advances on the clock interrupt. Running anything that raised the global timer resolution made it advance every 1 ms.
claims.evidence: Osenkov saw DateTime.UtcNow change only 3 times in 50 ms on one machine and 50 times on another. A commenter: "DateTime.UtcNow just uses the Win32 call GetSystemTimeAsFileTime ... the *precision* is actually 100ns ... but the accuracy is based on the timer interval (15.6ms or 1ms)". Another commenter: "multimedia timers are a common cause of seeing a lower resolution on some systems". A later comment links Lucas Hale's TimerResolution program "to modify the system timer".

claims.claim: The default tick of 15.625 ms (64 Hz) is the documented coarse clock. Microsoft's documented low-resolution APIs are GetTickCount64 and GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, which it says give 10 to 16 ms.
claims.evidence: Table row: "PC RTC | 64 Hz | 15.625 milliseconds". Also: "If resolution of 10 to 16 milliseconds is sufficient, you can use GetTickCount64 ... For UTC-synchronized time stamps, use GetSystemTimeAsFileTime".

claims.claim: Windows 10 version 2004 changed timeBeginPeriod. It no longer sets the timer resolution globally for every process, so one process can no longer reliably fix timer behavior for other processes.
claims.evidence: "Prior to Windows 10, version 2004, this function affects a global Windows setting... Starting with Windows 10, version 2004, this function no longer affects global timer resolution... For processes which have not called this function, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution."

claims.claim: Windows 11 adds a further rule: if a process owns a window that becomes occluded, minimized or invisible, its timer-resolution request may be ignored. A process can opt in to having its requests ignored through SetProcessInformation(ProcessPowerThrottling).
claims.evidence: "Starting with Windows 11, if a window-owning process becomes fully occluded, minimized, or otherwise invisible or inaudible to the end user, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution." SetProcessInformation: "When a process opts into enabling PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION, any current timer resolution requests made by the process will be ignored."

claims.claim: Even after the 2004 change, timeBeginPeriod still raises the hardware timer interrupt rate for the whole system. Only the guarantees to other processes changed, so any value tied to the interrupt can still be affected by other programs.
claims.evidence: "What this means is that timeBeginPeriod still sets the global timer interrupt interval, on all versions of Window." The post also says the change was undocumented when published and that Microsoft added one paragraph to the docs in 2021.

claims.claim: A registry value is reported to restore the old global timer-resolution behavior. Bruce Dawson, the blog's author, advises against using it except for testing.
claims.evidence: Reader comment (2022-12-20): DWORD GlobalTimerResolutionRequests=1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel, followed by a restart. Dawson: "I wouldn't recommend setting that (except for test purposes), and software definitely shouldn't set it on user machines." A Jan 2023 reader reported it worked only on Windows 11.

claims.claim: Measured on this machine today, the coarse system clock still follows whatever global interrupt rate another process has set. Something else on the machine currently holds the timer at 0.5 ms. Python's time.time_ns() and raw GetSystemTimeAsFileTime both stepped every ~500 us, whether or not the measuring process called timeBeginPeriod(1). So on current Windows 11 the old effect is still there: how often the coarse clock updates depends on what else is running.
claims.evidence: NtQueryTimerResolution: coarsest 15.625 ms, finest 0.5 ms, current 0.5 ms. Default run: time.time_ns median step 500.000 us (max 1003.2), GetSystemTimeAsFileTime median 500.1 us (max 1107.6). After timeBeginPeriod(1): the same (500.0 / 500.1 us medians).

claims.claim: The precise APIs do not depend on the tick at all. On the same machine, GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime stepped every ~0.4 us (the call cost) and the QPC frequency is 10 MHz (100 ns ticks).
claims.evidence: GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime: 1,147,654 distinct values in 0.5 s, median step 0.400 us. QueryPerformanceFrequency = 10000000. time.get_clock_info('perf_counter'): QueryPerformanceCounter(), resolution=1e-07.

claims.claim: On the project's Python 3.12, time.monotonic() uses GetTickCount64 and stepped every 16 ms even while the system timer was at 0.5 ms. time.get_clock_info('time') reports a resolution of 0.015625 even though the observed step was 0.5 ms, so the reported resolution is a nominal value only.
claims.evidence: time.monotonic_ns: 32 steps in 0.5 s, median 16000 us in both runs. get_clock_info('time') = implementation='GetSystemTimeAsFileTime()', resolution=0.015625. get_clock_info('monotonic') = 'GetTickCount64()', resolution=0.015625.

claims.claim: Python 3.13 moved time.time() and time.monotonic() on Windows onto the precise clocks, so on 3.13+ the 15.6 ms behavior goes away for these calls. The project allows Python >=3.11 and its .venv runs 3.12.
claims.evidence: "On Windows, monotonic() now uses the QueryPerformanceCounter() clock for a resolution of 1 microsecond, instead of the GetTickCount64() clock which has a resolution of 15.6 milliseconds." "On Windows, time() now uses the GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime() clock for a resolution of 1 microsecond, instead of the GetSystemTimeAsFileTime() clock which has a resolution of 15.6 milliseconds." pyproject.toml:5 requires-python = ">=3.11"; .python-version = 3.12.

claims.claim: The CPython issue asking for a precise time.time() on Windows was open for about 11 years before it was fixed. A maintainer's measurement there shows the coarse API at ~14 ms resolution.
claims.evidence: Issue opened 2013-09-12 by pitrou. vstinner (2015-07-31, Win 8.1 VM): "GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime(): 715 ns" vs "GetSystemTimeAsFileTime(): 14 ms". Fixed by PR #116822 "Use GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime() in time.time()".

claims.claim: Raising the timer resolution does nothing for QPC (time.perf_counter). QPC is Microsoft's recommended source for interval and event timestamps, and GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime is its recommendation for UTC timestamps.
claims.evidence: timeBeginPeriod doc: "Setting a higher resolution does not improve the accuracy of the high-resolution performance counter." Timestamps doc: "When you need time stamps with a resolution of 1 microsecond or better and you don't need the time stamps to be synchronized to an external time reference, choose QueryPerformanceCounter... When you need UTC-synchronized time stamps... choose GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime".

claims.claim: There were real Windows timer bugs, but they affected QPC on old hardware and Windows versions: non-invariant or unsynchronized TSCs before Vista, and the 'performance counter may unexpectedly leap forward' issue (KB274323). Microsoft says current Windows checks the TSC at boot and falls back to HPET or the ACPI PM timer, so applications do not need to work around it.
claims.evidence: "Systems with flawed firmware that run these versions of Windows [XP/2000] might not provide the same QPC reading on different cores". FAQ: "How do I determine and validate that QPC works on my machine? You don't need to perform such checks." "Is the performance counter monotonic (non-decreasing)? Yes." Mozilla bug 836869 (Win7/XP logs, fixed for mozilla23): QPC jumps "on minority of systems like 64-bit processors running 64-bit Windows XP".
claims.windows_version_or_scope: Windows XP/2000 (and some Win7) hardware; not current Win11

claims.claim: skellycam's per-frame timestamps use time.perf_counter_ns(), which is QPC, so the tick-rate issue does not affect them. Since Python 3.10, perf_counter on Windows uses the same clock in every process, so timestamps from the separate camera processes can be compared directly.
claims.evidence: opencv_get_frame.py:53-73 and opencv_camera_loop.py:36-159 all use time.perf_counter_ns(). Python docs: perf_counter "Changed in version 3.10: On Windows, the clock is now the same for all processes."

claims.claim: skellycam is affected in one place. TimebaseMapping gets its UTC anchor from time.time_ns(), which on the project's Python 3.12 is GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, so converting perf_counter to wall-clock time carries a constant offset error of up to one tick. That is up to ~0.5 ms on this machine right now, and up to ~15.6 ms if nothing else is raising the timer resolution. Each mapping instance gets a different offset. Relative frame timing is unaffected. Calling GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime through ctypes, or moving to Python 3.13+, would remove the error.
claims.evidence: timebase_mapping.py:22-23: utc_time_ns = field(default_factory=time.time_ns); perf_counter_ns = field(default_factory=time.perf_counter_ns). The local measurement shows time.time_ns stepping at the global interrupt interval (500 us here).

claims.claim: time.sleep no longer depends on timeBeginPeriod on Windows 10+ with Python 3.11+, because it uses a high-resolution waitable timer. Locally, time.sleep(0.001) took a median of ~1.5 ms.
claims.evidence: Python docs: "On Windows 10 and newer the implementation uses a high-resolution timer which provides resolution of 100 nanoseconds" ("Changed in version 3.11: ... On Windows, a waitable timer is now used."). Local: time.sleep(1ms) median 1.506 ms, max 1.535 ms (default) and median 1.504 ms, max 1.737 ms (after timeBeginPeriod(1)).

claims.claim: For long recordings, oscillator frequency error matters more than resolution. PC crystals are typically off by 30 to 50 ppm, which is several seconds per day relative to true time, unless timestamps are re-anchored to UTC.
claims.evidence: "Crystal oscillators that are used in personal computers and servers are typically manufactured with a frequency tolerance of ± 30 to 50 parts per million". "±50 ppm yields a maximum error of ± 4.3 seconds after 24 hours."

claims.claim: The behaviour the user heard about is real, but it was a design choice, not a bug. Windows wall-clock time (GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, which backs .NET DateTime.UtcNow and Python time.time() up to 3.12) only advances on the system timer interrupt. By default that interrupt runs at 64 Hz, so the clock jumps in steps of about 15.6 ms. Programs, typically C# programs, raised the interrupt rate by calling timeBeginPeriod or NtSetTimerResolution through P/Invoke so the clock would step every 1 ms.
claims.evidence: Kirill Osenkov (Microsoft blog, 2012-05-16): DateTime.UtcNow 'only updated 3 times within a 50 millisecond interval' on one machine, but 50 times on another. Comment by James Manning: 'DateTime.UtcNow just uses the Win32 call GetSystemTimeAsFileTime ... the precision is actually 100ns ... but the accuracy is based on the timer interval (15.6ms or 1ms)... ClockRes ... Maximum timer interval: 15.600 ms ... Current timer interval: 1.000 ms'. Another comment: 'multimedia timers are a common cause of seeing a lower resolution on some systems'. A later commenter links 'a little program I wrote to modify the system timer'.

claims.claim: Microsoft documents the default timer tick as 64 Hz (15.625 ms). It recommends QueryPerformanceCounter for interval timestamps and GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime (Windows 8+, under 1 µs) for UTC timestamps. GetSystemTimeAsFileTime is listed among the APIs with 10 to 16 ms resolution.
claims.evidence: 'PC RTC | 64 Hz | 15.625 milliseconds'; 'If resolution of 10 to 16 milliseconds is sufficient, you can use GetTickCount64, QueryInterruptTime ... For UTC-synchronized time stamps, use GetSystemTimeAsFileTime'; 'When you need UTC-synchronized time stamps with a resolution of 1 microsecond or better, choose GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime'

claims.claim: The fix for imprecise wall-clock time is GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime, added in Windows 8 and Server 2012. It does not depend on the timer tick, so code no longer needs to raise the timer rate just to get a finer clock.
claims.evidence: 'retrieves the current system date and time with the highest possible level of precision (<1us)'; Minimum supported client: Windows 8

claims.claim: There were also real QPC/TSC hardware problems, but they belong to the XP era and Windows now handles them itself. On Windows XP and 2000, some multi-core systems with a non-invariant or unsynchronised TSC gave different QPC readings on different cores. From Windows 7 on, Windows checks the TSC at boot and switches to HPET or the ACPI PM timer when the TSC is unsuitable. Microsoft says applications need no workaround such as pinning thread affinity or checking the TSC themselves.
claims.evidence: 'some multi-core or multi-processor systems used processors with TSCs that couldn't be synchronized across cores. Systems with flawed firmware that run these versions of Windows might not provide the same QPC reading on different cores'; 'How do I determine and validate that QPC works on my machine? You don't need to perform such checks.'; 'Do I need to set the thread affinity to a single core to use QPC? No.'; 'Is the performance counter monotonic (non-decreasing)? Yes.'
claims.windows_version_or_scope: Problem: XP/2000 on flawed firmware. Fixed: Vista/7 onward

claims.claim: Windows 10 version 2004 changed timeBeginPeriod. It used to be global: any process that raised the rate raised it for every process. It is now effectively per-process, so a program that relied on some other app (a browser, a media player) having raised the rate no longer gets fast timers.
claims.evidence: 'Prior to Windows 10, version 2004, this function affects a global Windows setting... Starting with Windows 10, version 2004, this function no longer affects global timer resolution... For processes which have not called this function, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution.' Also: 'Setting a higher resolution does not improve the accuracy of the high-resolution performance counter.'

claims.claim: Windows 11 added another restriction. A window-owning process that is fully occluded, minimized, invisible or inaudible may have its timer-resolution request ignored. A process can opt out with SetProcessInformation(ProcessPowerThrottling), clearing PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION in ControlMask with StateMask=0, which tells Windows to 'Always honor Timer Resolution Requests'.
claims.evidence: 'By default in Windows 11 if a window owning process becomes fully occluded, minimized, or otherwise non-visible to the end user, and non-audible, Windows may automatically ignore the timer resolution request and thus does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution.' Example code: 'Always honor Timer Resolution Requests... ControlMask = PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION; StateMask = 0'

claims.claim: According to Bruce Dawson, timeBeginPeriod still raises the global hardware interrupt rate after 2004, so clocks driven by the tick (system time, timeGetTime) still update faster for everyone. What changed is that the scheduler only wakes the requesting processes at the faster rate. He measured irregular Sleep(1) wake-ups and called the inconsistency 'worrisome'.
claims.evidence: 'timeBeginPeriod still sets the global timer interrupt interval, on all versions of Window'; 'the interrupt fires on at least one CPU core at that rate, and the time is updated'; 'However the scheduler behavior changes dramatically in Windows 10 2004'; the test program 'was only waking up about 64 times a second instead of the 500 times a second'; 'Sleep(1) when another process has called timeBeginPeriod(8) returns after one interval about 20% of the time and after two intervals the rest'; 'Update, 2021: this change is acknowledged now in the timeBeginPeriod documentation.'

claims.claim: The 'registry' version of the fix is probably the undocumented GlobalTimerResolutionRequests value. Set to 1 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\kernel (reboot required), it is reported to restore the old global timeBeginPeriod behaviour on Windows 11 and Server 2022. Microsoft does not document it, Dawson advises against it except for testing, and the TimerResolution tool says 'This should only be used for debugging purposes.' It is not set on this machine.
claims.evidence: Dawson post comments: commenter gives GlobalTimerResolutionRequests DWORD 1; author would not recommend it except for testing. valleyofdoom README: 'the registry key below can also be used so that requesting a higher resolution is effective on a system-wide level ... This should only be used for debugging purposes.' Local `reg query` of that key lists only DpcWatchdogProfileOffset, ObUnsecureGlobalNames, SeTokenSingletonAttributesConfig and obcaseinsensitive, with no GlobalTimerResolutionRequests.

Closed as completed via coreclr#9736 on 2017-02-24. Vance Morrison recommended making UtcNow more precise at a '2-3X slower' cost; stephentoub '+1'. claims.claim: Python's time.time() used the coarse GetSystemTimeAsFileTime until Python 3.13, which switched it to GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime. skellycam's venv runs Python 3.12.13, so time.time()/time_ns() still use the coarse API. On 3.12, time.monotonic() is GetTickCount64 (16 ms steps measured), and perf_counter() is QPC with 100 ns resolution (QPF = 10 MHz).

CPython gh-63207, opened 2013-09-12: vstinner measured 'GetSystemTimeAsFileTime(): 14 ms' vs 'GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime(): 715 ns' on Windows 8.1. Local .venv: time.get_clock_info('time') -> implementation='GetSystemTimeAsFileTime()', resolution=0.015625; monotonic -> 'GetTickCount64()'; perf_counter -> 'QueryPerformanceCounter()', resolution=1e-07.

claims.claim: Measured on this Windows 11 machine (build 26300), the old behaviour is still there in the coarse APIs. GetSystemTimeAsFileTime advances in steps set by the current global timer interrupt, which some other process has raised to 0.5 ms, so the steps are a median 0.5 ms and at most 1.02 ms. GetTickCount64 still steps about every 16 ms, and GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime steps about every 0.4 µs. Calling timeBeginPeriod(1) in our own process changed nothing, because the global rate was already 0.5 ms. Sleep(1) took a median of 1.5 ms (1.0 to 2.5 ms) in both Python and PowerShell, even before either process requested a faster timer. So on this build, a process that did not ask got sub-2 ms sleeps, not the 15.6 ms Dawson describes for 2004. The cause was not determined.

claims.claim: For skellycam, the per-frame timestamps are not affected. They use time.perf_counter_ns() (QPC), and timer-resolution settings do not touch QPC. The only exposure is the one-time TimebaseMapping anchor, which pairs time.time_ns() with perf_counter_ns. On Python 3.12 that anchor can be off by up to one timer tick (0.5 to 1 ms here, up to about 15.6 ms on an idle machine). The error is a constant offset for the whole recording and does not change the spacing between frames. Using Python 3.13+, or reading GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime directly for the anchor, removes it.

Python 3.11+ on Windows 10+ implements time.sleep with a high-resolution waitable timer, so it is not tied to the 15.6 ms tick the way Sleep() is. Windowless camera child processes are not covered by the Windows 11 occlusion rule, which applies to window-owning processes, but a GUI process that does timing-sensitive waits while minimized could be.

On Windows, a waitable timer is now used.' wait_functions.py lines 23-33 define wait_1ms/100us/10us/1us via time.sleep.

It reads MFSampleExtension_DeviceReferenceSystemTime (falling back to MFGetSystemTime()) only to compute capture_begin_time. That value is forwarded only when the kMediaFoundationVideoCaptureForwardSampleTimestamps feature is enabled, and that feature is FEATURE_DISABLED_BY_DEFAULT.

The capture pin (Smart Tee output 0) keeps its timestamps.
verified.note: The quotes are exact. This is a consequence of how a DS graph is built (use the capture pin), not a limit of DS itself, so it favours neither stack.

verified.claim: OpenCV CAP_DSHOW discards DS timestamps: PREVIEW-pin graph, NULL sync source, SampleTime ignored, RGB24 forced (decoder inserted); so CAP_DSHOW timing problems are OpenCV's design.

The grabber is set to MEDIASUBTYPE_RGB24 unless the source is a single-byte format, Y16 or NV12, so MJPG sources get a decoder inserted. CAP_DSHOW's lack of timestamps is a property of OpenCV's graph, not of DirectShow.

MF-side flakiness, local: twice, MF briefly could not find the generic camera right after a USB bandwidth refusal (research/usb_cameras/docs/mjpeg_passthrough_summary.md, camera-health section).

Frame Server reliability reports: (a) Microsoft Q&A, 2023-10-30, Windows 11 22H2 with a Logitech C920. The Frame Server Monitor crashed several times a minute (KERNELBASE C++ exception), and the thread was locked unresolved: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/4102987/windows-camera-frame-server-monitor-continually-cr . (b) Microsoft Q&A, 2024-07-16, Windows 11. IMFActivate::ActivateObject occasionally froze for 5-10 minutes after cameras were plugged in often, leaving every camera unusable until the wait ended or the PC rebooted; no fix was given: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1819830/why-does-the-interface-get-stuck-for-5-10-minutes . Both are relevant to one process per camera with hot-plugging, and both are MF/Frame Server failure modes that a non-bridged DS path might avoid.

Local timing evidence the report left out: the DirectShow device sample times returned through PyAV/FFmpeg are constant to 100 ns (333333 on the C922), so they are synthesized, not measured. MF IMFSample times (seen through SDL3) and all host arrival times fall on an approximately 16 ms grid, which limits them to about ±8 ms. Only the UVC PTS/SCR, which reached MF after a one-time admin registry value was set, gave about 0.4-1.8 ms error. MF's timing advantage therefore comes from UVC metadata access, not from MF sample timestamps. Sources: research/usb_cameras/prior_art/SURVEY.md:50,56-69; research/usb_cameras/docs/usb_camera_report.md:40-58; research/REPORT.md:29.

Native-JPEG MF paths that need no compiling, measured locally: GStreamer 1.28 mfvideosrc (pip gstreamer-bundle) and SDL3 3.4.18's MF camera API both delivered 100% valid native JPEG. SDL3 also did so on the Kiyo Pro, where PyAV dshow fell back to YUY2 rawvideo (research/usb_cameras/prior_art/SURVEY.md:48-53).

The UVC Camera Implementation Guide says devices that publish UVC-CPV2FaceAuth do not need EnableDshowRedirection to be bridged; it is still required for older Windows or for MJPEG decoding in Frame Server. So the bridge opt-in is not the only route (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/stream/uvc-camera-implementation-guide).

On this machine, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OEM\DshowBridge\1 (and the WOW6432Node copy) has Application=Launcher_Main.exe, Productname=Logitech Camera Software, and mfksproxy.dll references the 'Application' and 'ProductName' values. DS-to-MF bridging therefore appears to also be controlled per application, a mechanism that is undocumented.

The same Microsoft maintainer comment that calls DS legacy also says 'Some apps do still support DShow sources in some capacity such as Teams, Skype, Zoom', and that DS-filter virtual cameras 'can incur issues if modified from 1 client while concurrently used from another' (https://github.com/microsoft/Windows-Camera/issues/72, 2024-11-19).

Chromium also blocks MF+D3D11 for two USB webcams (05a3:9331, 04f2:b6bf) because 'MFCaptureEngine fails with E_MF_SAMPLEALLOCATOREMPTY', and blocks 'VMware Virtual Webcam' because it hangs under MF. Separately, the MF path's device-QPC capture_begin_time forwarding (kMediaFoundationVideoCaptureForwardSampleTimestamps) is disabled by default (video_capture_device_factory_win.cc l.172-184; video_capture_device_mf_win.cc l.57).

Relevant to the user's relayed question about the Windows timer: this verification step did not research it, but the evidence bears on it. The ~16 ms arrival/sample-time grid measured locally matches the default Windows timer tick of 15.625 ms. Microsoft's timeBeginPeriod doc says that before Windows 10 2004 the call set a global timer resolution. From 2004 on it affects only the calling process ('Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution' for other processes). From Windows 11, a window-owning process that is fully occluded, minimized or invisible may lose the higher resolution (see SetProcessInformation, PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION). The old practice of running a helper program that raises the resolution for every process therefore no longer works on current Windows; each capture process must request it itself (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/timeapi/nf-timeapi-timebeginperiod, updated 2024-02-22). Whether the 16 ms camera grid is caused by the timer tick or by USB/usbvideo.sys completion timing has not been tested (SURVEY.md lists the latter as an unverified hypothesis).

A commenter explained that DateTime.UtcNow calls GetSystemTimeAsFileTime: precision is 100 ns, but accuracy follows the timer interval (15.6 ms or 1 ms). The commenter's ClockRes output showed a Win7 SP1 machine at 1 ms. Commenters named multimedia timers as a common cause of the higher rate and powercfg /energy as a way to find which program is responsible. A later comment links Lucas Hale's tool 'to modify the system timer'. The source never uses the word 'bug'; calling it designed behavior is an inference, though a well-supported one.

For processes which have not called this function, Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution.' Before 2004 it was a global setting. What changed is the guarantee to other processes. In practice the interrupt rate is still global (see claims 5 and 7).

It also says that by default in Windows 11 'Windows may automatically ignore the timer resolution request' of such a process.

Within a camera group a single mapping is shared: process_and_save_recording_timestamps.py:59-64 checks that every frame's mapping is identical. So cameras in one recording share the same offset. audio_recorder.py:169 creates its own TimebaseMapping(), so audio and video UTC anchors can differ by up to one tick. verified.corrected_claim: Microsoft's doc: PC crystals are 'typically manufactured with a frequency tolerance of ± 30 to 50 parts per million, and rarely... as much as 500 ppm'; '±50 ppm yields a maximum error of ± 4.3 seconds after 24 hours'. The same page says recent Windows versions, especially Windows 8, use multiple hardware timers at boot to detect the frequency offset and compensate for it as far as possible. So the uncompensated 30-50 ppm figure is a worst-case bound, not the expected residual error.
verified.note: The report left out the boot-time calibration sentence, which lowers the expected drift. For a few cameras on one PC all reading the same QPC, drift does not affect relative sync between cameras. It matters only when comparing with UTC or with other machines.

missed: Modern .NET no longer has the coarse DateTime.UtcNow behavior at the center of the 'run some C# code' story. dotnet/runtime src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/DateTime.Windows.cs uses GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime when it exists and agrees with GetSystemTimeAsFileTime to within 100 ms. Its own comment warns that 'on misconfigured systems, it's possible for the "precise" time to be inaccurate'. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dotnet/runtime/main/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/DateTime.Windows.cs (read 2026-10-28). The proposal was dotnet/coreclr #5883 (2016). The exact .NET release that shipped the switch was not confirmed, and .NET Framework 4.x behavior was not checked. On current Windows 11 with current .NET, the C# 15.6 ms symptom is mostly gone unless the code runs on .NET Framework.

No register is involved. The 'C# code to make the timer update' was almost certainly a program calling timeBeginPeriod or NtSetTimerResolution (for example Lucas Hale's TimerResolution, or the 'timer resolution' rules in Process Lasso: https://bitsum.com/apps/process-lasso/docs/rules/timer-resolution/). Process Lasso documents that since Win10 2004 such an adjustment has no effect on processes that do not request a resolution themselves 'unless you have checked Apply globally'. This partly contradicts the local finding that GetSystemTimeAsFileTime still follows another process's rate. Process Lasso is talking about timer and wait expiry, not time-of-day updates, so the two claims are about different things and both can hold.

The 'Windows 11 rule' may matter for skellycam: the docs say requests from occluded or minimized window-owning processes may be ignored. If the program that currently holds 0.5 ms (unidentified; it could be a browser, Razer or LogiTune software, etc.) gets minimized or closed, coarse clocks on this machine fall back to 15.625 ms. So the 0.5 ms observed today is not a stable property of the machine. Source: timeBeginPeriod and SetProcessInformation docs above.

Windows Internals, as quoted by a 2023-03-24 comment on Dawson's post: modern Windows 10 'no longer necessarily run on a periodic tick' (dynamic tick). How often the coarse clock updates can therefore also vary with idle state, not only with resolution requests. Not verified against the book itself. Source: https://randomascii.wordpress.com/2020/10/04/windows-timer-resolution-the-great-rule-change/ (comments).

No evidence found of any current Windows 11 bug in which the system time 'fails to update at regular intervals'. Searches for 22H2, 23H2 or 24H2 timer or GetSystemTimeAsFileTime regressions returned nothing specific. Dawson's comments up to 2025 contain no Windows 11 timing regressions beyond the registry-key anecdote.

The report did not note that Python 3.13 also makes perf_counter the same clock as monotonic ('Changed in version 3.13: Use the same clock as time.monotonic()'). That is harmless for skellycam, because both are QPC on 3.13. https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html

verified.claim: The behaviour was a design choice, not a bug. GetSystemTimeAsFileTime (behind .NET DateTime.UtcNow and Python time.time() up to 3.12) only advances on the system timer interrupt, which defaults to 64 Hz (about 15.6 ms steps). Programs, typically C#, raised the rate with timeBeginPeriod or NtSetTimerResolution via P/Invoke to get 1 ms steps.
verified.corrected_claim: A 2012 Microsoft blog post (Kirill Osenkov) measured DateTime.UtcNow changing only 3 times in 50 ms on one machine and 50 times on another. A commenter (James Manning, not the blog author) explained that UtcNow wraps GetSystemTimeAsFileTime. Its precision is 100 ns, but its accuracy follows the current timer interval: 15.6 ms by default, or 1 ms when some program has raised it. ClockRes showed max 15.600 ms, min 0.500 ms, current 1.000 ms on his Win7 SP1 machine. Another comment names multimedia timers as a common cause of the higher rate. A later commenter links a utility (lucashale.com) that changes the system timer. The post does not mention C#/P/Invoke code to fix it, NtSetTimerResolution or the registry. 'Design choice, not a bug' is the gatherer's characterisation.
verified.strength: maintainer-statement (actually a reader comment on an MS employee blog)
verified.note: The quotes match. The strength label is overstated: the explanatory text is an anonymous/reader comment that corrected the author. Scope is Win7/Server 2008 R2 and .NET Framework, and .NET has since changed (see the .NET claim). 'Typically C# programs ... via P/Invoke' is not in the source and is inference.

verified.claim: Microsoft documents the default timer tick as 64 Hz (15.625 ms), recommends QPC for intervals and GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime (Win8+, <1 us) for UTC, and lists GetSystemTimeAsFileTime among the 10-16 ms resolution APIs.
verified.corrected_claim: The 'Acquiring high-resolution time stamps' page has a clock-source table row 'PC RTC | 64 Hz | 15.625 milliseconds'. It does not explicitly call this the default system timer tick, although the 15.625 ms coarsest resolution matches NtQueryTimerResolution on this machine. The page recommends QPC for interval timestamps and GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime for UTC timestamps of 1 us or better. It says that if 10 to 16 ms resolution is enough, GetTickCount64/QueryInterruptTime etc. can be used, and 'For UTC-synchronized time stamps, use GetSystemTimeAsFileTime'. It frames that fallback mainly as the cheap option on platforms where high-resolution counters are expensive.
verified.note: All quotes are verbatim. The only overreach is calling the RTC table row 'the default timer tick'.

verified.claim: GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime (Windows 8 / Server 2012) is the fix. It does not depend on the timer tick, so code no longer needs to raise the timer rate to get a finer clock.
verified.corrected_claim: GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime 'retrieves the current system date and time with the highest possible level of precision (<1us)' in UTC. Minimum client is Windows 8, minimum server Windows Server 2012. Its independence from the timer tick is not stated on the page, but local measurement backs it: about 0.4 us steps, against 0.5 ms steps for GetSystemTimeAsFileTime at the same moment.
verified.note: The page also says to use QPC, not this function, for high-resolution interval measurements.

verified.claim: QPC/TSC hardware problems belonged to the XP era. From Windows 7 on, Windows checks the TSC at boot and falls back to HPET or ACPI PM timer, and apps need no workaround (affinity pinning, TSC checks).
verified.corrected_claim: The MS doc says XP/2000 systems with flawed firmware (non-invariant TSC, or TSCs not synchronised across cores) 'might not provide the same QPC reading on different cores'. Vista/Server 2008 always used HPET or the PM timer. From Windows 7, Windows uses the TSC only when it can synchronise it, and otherwise automatically selects HPET or the PM timer. 'During system initialization, Windows checks if the TSC is suitable.' The FAQ says no validation is needed, thread affinity is 'neither necessary nor desirable', and QPC 'does not go backward'. QPC values from different threads have a ±1 tick ordering ambiguity.
verified.note: Accurate. The fix arguably dates from Vista (platform counter everywhere), with Win7 adding safe TSC use. The report omits the separate XP-era 'QPC leaps forward' chipset bug (KB274323), which apps really did work around in code (see missed).

verified.claim: Windows 10 2004 made timeBeginPeriod effectively per-process, so a program that relied on another app raising the rate no longer gets fast timers.
verified.corrected_claim: The timeBeginPeriod doc says that before Windows 10 2004 the function affected a global setting, and from 2004 it 'no longer affects global timer resolution'. Processes that call it get the lowest value requested by any calling process, so it is not strictly per-process. For processes that have not called it, 'Windows does not guarantee a higher resolution than the default system resolution'. The doc also says 'Setting a higher resolution does not improve the accuracy of the high-resolution performance counter.' The doc promises no guarantee, not a hard loss: on this Windows 11 build 26300.9711 machine, a process that never called timeBeginPeriod still got Sleep(1) of about 1.5 ms (re-measured by the verifier).
verified.note: Quotes verified. 'No longer gets fast timers' overstates the doc's 'does not guarantee' and is contradicted by the local measurement in the report's own Windows 11 claim.

verified.claim: Windows 11 may ignore timer-resolution requests from a window-owning process that is occluded, minimized, invisible or inaudible. Opt out with SetProcessInformation(ProcessPowerThrottling), ControlMask=PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION, StateMask=0.
verified.corrected_claim: SetProcessInformation doc: 'By default in Windows 11 if a window owning process becomes fully occluded, minimized, or otherwise non-visible to the end user, and non-audible, Windows may automatically ignore the timer resolution request.' Its example 'Always honor Timer Resolution Requests' sets ControlMask = PROCESS_POWER_THROTTLING_IGNORE_TIMER_RESOLUTION and StateMask = 0. The timeBeginPeriod doc words the condition as 'invisible or inaudible', so the two MS pages disagree on and/or. Per SetProcessInformation it is non-visible AND non-audible.
verified.note: The report's claim text says 'or inaudible', while its evidence quote says 'and non-audible'. Minor inconsistency between the two MS docs.

verified.claim: Per Bruce Dawson, timeBeginPeriod still raises the global interrupt rate after 2004, so tick-driven clocks update faster for everyone. Only scheduler wake-ups changed. He measured irregular Sleep(1) and called it 'worrisome'.

A non-calling test program woke 'about 64 times a second instead of the 500 times a second' it would have under earlier Windows. Sleep(1), when another process had called timeBeginPeriod(8), returned after one interval about 20% of the time and after two the rest. He wrote that 'the intentional inconsistency in the Sleep(1) delays is particularly worrisome'. A 2021 update notes the doc now acknowledges the change. The article does not name GetSystemTimeAsFileTime. That system time steps faster in non-calling processes is supported by local measurement (0.5 ms steps here), not by the article text.

Dawson advises against it except for testing, and the TimerResolution README says debugging only. Not set on this machine.
verified.corrected_claim: Community sources only. A reader comment on Dawson's post says the DWORD GlobalTimerResolutionRequests=1 worked on Windows 11 but not Windows 10. Dawson replied it would likely apply to Windows 10 or 11 and that he would not recommend it except for testing, and software should not set it on user machines. The valleyofdoom/TimerResolution README says that 'on Windows Server 2022+ and Windows 11+' the key makes requests system-wide, attributes this to that Dawson comment, and says 'This should only be used for debugging purposes.' A verifier `reg query` on this machine shows only DpcWatchdogProfileOffset, ObUnsecureGlobalNames, SeTokenSingletonAttributesConfig and obcaseinsensitive, so the value is not set. No Microsoft documentation found.

verified.claim: skellycam per-frame timestamps use perf_counter_ns (QPC) and are unaffected. The only exposure is the one-time TimebaseMapping time.time_ns anchor (up to one tick off), a constant offset for the whole recording that does not change frame spacing. Python 3.13+ or GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime removes it.
verified.corrected_claim: Frame grab/retrieve timestamps are perf_counter_ns (opencv_get_frame.py:53-73, opencv_camera_loop.py), so frame spacing is independent of timer resolution. One TimebaseMapping is shared by the camera group (camera_group_ipc.py:24, default_factory=TimebaseMapping), so on Python 3.12 its UTC anchor can be off by up to one system-time step (0.5-1 ms here, up to ~15.6 ms on an idle machine), the same for all cameras. Three caveats. (1) The offset is constant only relative to the anchor. Because QPC is not NTP-disciplined, perf-counter-derived UTC drifts from true UTC at the crystal's ppm error (MS doc: ±10 ppm ≈ ±36 ms/hour; PC crystals are typically ±30-50 ppm), which matters for multi-hour recordings or cross-machine sync. (2) AudioRecorder creates its own TimebaseMapping (audio_recorder.py:38), so audio and video UTC anchors can differ by up to one step. Raw perf_counter_ns stays comparable on Windows. (3) recording_start_timestamp uses FullTimestamp.now(), which calls datetime.now(), another coarse-clock read on 3.12 (full_timestamp.py:76, recording_info.py:24).
verified.note: The core point holds, but 'constant offset for the whole recording' ignores QPC-vs-UTC drift, and the report missed the second (audio) anchor and the datetime.now() use.

verified.claim: Timer resolution still matters for waits. skellycam's wait helpers sleep 1 ms/100 us/10 us/1 us. Python 3.11+ on Win10+ uses a high-resolution waitable timer, so it is not tied to the 15.6 ms tick the way Sleep() is. Windowless camera child processes are not covered by the Win11 occlusion rule.
verified.corrected_claim: Python docs: on Windows 10 and newer, time.sleep 'uses a high-resolution timer which provides resolution of 100 nanoseconds', and since 3.11 'a waitable timer is now used'. wait_functions.py:23-33 defines wait_1ms/100us/10us/1us via time.sleep. In the verifier's measurement on this machine, the sub-millisecond helpers do not sleep for their stated time: time.sleep(1e-4), (1e-5) and (1e-6) each took a median ~0.50 ms (min ~0.43-0.45 ms), and time.sleep(1e-3) took a median 1.51 ms (1.02-1.89). The floor matches the 0.5 ms finest timer resolution, so 'resolution of 100 ns' is the API unit, not the achieved wake precision. Whether the camera child processes own windows, and so fall outside the Win11 occlusion rule, is an inference and was not checked.
verified.note: Weakened because the claim implies sub-ms waits work as named. Locally they are 5x-500x longer than named. The occlusion exemption for child processes is unverified.

missed: Another reading of the user's story is the Windows 8+ 'dynamic tick' (tickless timer). The timer interrupt deliberately stops firing at regular intervals when the system is idle. Microsoft's BCDEdit reference lists 'disabledynamictick [yes|no] Enables and disables dynamic timer tick feature' and 'useplatformclock'/'useplatformtick', each marked 'This option should only be used for debugging'. Gaming and tweak forums still recommend toggling these, with mixed, anecdotal results. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/devtest/bcdedit--set (updated 2024-04-29); https://forums.blurbusters.com/viewtopic.php?p=110585

The user's 'register' may mean a hardware counter rather than the registry. The XP-era 'Performance counter value may unexpectedly leap forward' bug (Microsoft KB274323) made QueryPerformanceCounter jump on certain chipsets, and real projects shipped code workarounds (pjproject, PortAudio ticket, Mozilla leap-detection heuristic). This is a genuine Windows timer bug that needed application code, unlike the timer-resolution design behaviour. It is XP/2003-era and superseded by the Vista+ QPC design. Sources: https://gitea.sysmocom.de/sysmocom/pjproject/commit/e2eea447d0ab6bdd649782f7db92691e99740392 ; https://www.assembla.com/spaces/portaudio/tickets/133 ; https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=836869

Python 3.13 also changed time.monotonic() on Windows from GetTickCount64 (~16 ms steps) to QueryPerformanceCounter, and perf_counter now uses the same clock. Upgrading to 3.13 fixes both time.time() and time.monotonic(), not just time.time(). websocket_server.py:242 uses time.monotonic(), which steps every ~16 ms on the current 3.12 venv. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html (clock section: 'On Windows, call QueryPerformanceCounter()'; perf_counter 'Changed in version 3.13: Use the same clock as monotonic()').

QPC drift relative to UTC: Microsoft's own table gives ±36 ms per hour at ±10 ppm and notes PC crystals are typically ±30-50 ppm. A one-time perf_counter->UTC anchor therefore drifts from NTP-corrected wall time over long recordings, which matters if skellycam UTC timestamps are compared with other machines or devices. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/acquiring-high-resolution-time-stamps

Measured locally by the verifier: skellycam's wait_100us/wait_10us/wait_1us all sleep ~0.5 ms (median 499 us), and wait_1ms sleeps ~1.5 ms median, with the global timer already at 0.5 ms. On an idle machine with no timer-raising app the floor may differ. Any loop that relies on these helpers for sub-ms pacing is about 5x-500x slower than the names suggest. The Windows build is 10.0.26300.9711. All 'current Windows 11' conclusions in the report rest on this single build and machine. If 26300 is an Insider/Dev-channel build rather than GA (24H2 = 26100, 25H2 = 26200), the Sleep(1)-without-timeBeginPeriod result may not represent shipping Windows 11. This was not checked against a GA build.

Not opened in detail, so treat as leads.
